vignette:
Mariana arrived at the clinic on a Tuesday evening, straight from a twelve-hour shift at the boutique hotel she managed in downtown Miami. She was thirty-seven, a slim woman with dark hair pulled into a tight ponytail, and she spoke in quick, clipped sentences, as if she were afraid a pause would let something slip. It took her three tries to say why she had come. “I can’t keep doing this,” she finally managed, and then she went silent, her hands pressed flat against her thighs. She had grown up in a Cuban-American household in Hialeah, where her abuela still lived two blocks from the house Mariana had shared with her parents before they returned to the island. The Spanish she spoke with her grandmother was the language of comfort and expectation—her abuela had raised her to be fuerte, to hold the family together, to never bring shame on them. That voice now echoed whenever the memory surfaced: *You should have known better. You should have fought harder.* She had never told her abuela what happened, and the thought of doing so filled her with a dread far worse than the physical memory.

The assault had happened two years earlier, in a windowless back office of the hotel’s conference wing. A regional sales representative, someone she had exchanged pleasantries with at quarterly meetings, had cornered her after a late event and forced himself on her. Mariana could still feel the drywall against her shoulder blades, the sting of his grip on her wrist, the way the fluorescent light flickered above them. But she could not, for the life of her, arrange these pieces into a story she could hold in her mind. Whenever she tried to tell herself what had happened, the words scattered. She knew it was real—her body knew—but her memory was a series of jagged shards, each one suffused with a shame so deep it made her cheeks burn. She had never spoken the event aloud to anyone, not even her partner. She could not find a shape for it, only a feeling of wrongness that clung to her like a second skin. The silence felt like loyalty to her family’s code—*no se habla de esas cosas*—but it also felt like a cage.

In the months that followed, Mariana developed a simple rule: stay busy. She began arriving at the hotel before dawn and leaving after dark, taking on extra shifts, volunteering to cover other managers’ vacations. At first it felt like competence—she was the most reliable person on the payroll—but soon it became a need. If she slowed down, if she sat still for even a few minutes, the thoughts would find her: loops of what she should have done, what she could have said, fantasies of confronting the man in the parking lot, of making him pay. The revenge scenarios were vivid and exhausting, and they filled the quiet hours she had once used to decompress. Overwork was the only way to keep them at bay. She also learned to scan every face that walked through the lobby, cataloging men by build, hair color, the slope of their shoulders. Any man who matched the profile made her stomach drop, and she would delegate front-desk interactions to her staff, retreating to the back office. She stopped attending the quarterly industry meetings, claiming scheduling conflicts. Her partner—a white man from Ohio who could not understand why she flinched when he touched her unexpectedly—noticed she no longer wanted to go out on weekend evenings. When he asked why, she blamed exhaustion, but what she really felt was a deep certainty that the danger was still out there, that it could happen again because there was something fundamentally wrong with her.

What frightened Mariana most was the conviction that the assault had happened because of who she was. She was not a victim of circumstance; she was the kind of person this sort of thing happened to. There was something broken in her, something the attacker had sensed, and her body now confirmed this every day. Her heart would race at a harmless sound—the clatter of a cart in the hallway, a door closing too hard—and she would think, *See? You are still on edge, still weak, still the person who froze instead of fighting.* She had come to believe that her own physiology was a traitor, reacting as if the threat were still present, proving that she had never truly been safe and never would be. The hypervigilance was constant: she checked the locks on her apartment door three times before bed, she avoided certain corridors in the hotel, and she never let herself walk alone after dark, even to her car. Her abuela would call on Sundays and ask why she sounded so tired, and Mariana would lie and say work was busy.

She finally sought help because the overwork was no longer holding. Last week, at two in the morning, after a sixteen-hour day, she had found herself standing in front of the hotel’s walk-in freezer, considering how it would feel to simply sit down inside it and let the cold take over. It was not a plan, she insisted—just a thought. But it had scared her enough to call a therapist the next morning. Now, in the office, she could not quite bring herself to say that part aloud. Instead she whispered, “I need to find a way to live with what happened, but I don’t even know what that means. I can’t even tell you the story. All I have is the shame, and the way my body keeps screaming at me.” She looked down at her hands, still pressed flat against her thighs, and admitted she was terrified she would spend the rest of her life running from something she could not name—and that her abuela would someday find out, and the disappointment would be worse than anything the attacker had done.
